title: Equations of Motion
short_intro: The equations of motion describe the kinematic behavior of objects under the influence of applied forces without necessarily referencing the causes of motion. They establish rigorous analytical relationships between displacement, velocity, acceleration, and time for systems under constant or variable acceleration.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Derivation and application of kinematic equations for rectilinear motion with uniform acceleration, motion under gravity, relative velocity, and graphical analysis of distance-time and velocity-time graphs.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Generalized motion under variable acceleration using calculus, motion in a plane (projectile motion), constrained motion, and rotational analogues of equations of motion.

prerequisites: Scalar and vector calculus (differentiation and integration)
Concept of instantaneous velocity and acceleration

concept_notes.heading: Kinematics of Uniform Acceleration
bullets: Acceleration is maintained strictly constant with respect to time, a = constant.
The average velocity over a time interval equals the arithmetic mean of initial and final velocities only under uniform acceleration.
Dimensions of all terms in the kinematic equations must be dimensionally homogeneous (L for displacement, LT^-1 for velocity, LT^-2 for acceleration).

concept_notes.heading: Motion Under Gravity
bullets: Free-fall acceleration g acts downward toward the center of the Earth, conventionally taken as g = 9.8 m/s^2.
Air resistance is neglected in standard elementary formulations, making the magnitude of acceleration identical during ascent and descent.
Time of ascent equals time of descent for an object projected vertically upward and returning to the same horizontal level.

concept_notes.heading: Calculus Formulations for Variable Acceleration
bullets: When acceleration is a function of time t, position x, or velocity v, calculus is required: a = dv/dt = v (dv/dx).
Velocity is obtained by integrating the acceleration-time function: v(t) = v_0 + int a(t) dt.
Displacement is obtained by integrating the velocity-time function: x(t) = x_0 + int v(t) dt.

concept_notes.heading: Relative Motion in One and Two Dimensions
bullets: The velocity of particle A relative to particle B is given by v_{AB} = v_A - v_B.
Galilean transformation links coordinates between an inertial frame and a frame moving with constant velocity relative to it.
In frames experiencing linear acceleration or rotation, pseudo-forces (such as the Coriolis force) must be factored into the equations of motion.

derivations.title: Derivation of Kinematic Equations using Calculus
derivations.conditions: Acceleration 'a' is constant, motion is along a straight line.
steps: Start with the definition of acceleration: a =  rac{dv}{dt}.
Rearrange and integrate both sides from time t = 0 (velocity v_0) to time t (velocity v): int_{v_0}^{v} dv = int_{0}^{t} a dt.
Evaluate the integral: v - v_0 = at Rightarrow v = v_0 + at.
Substitute v =  rac{dx}{dt} into the velocity equation:  rac{dx}{dt} = v_0 + at.
Integrate for displacement from x = 0 at t = 0 to x at time t: int_{0}^{x} dx = int_{0}^{t} (v_0 + at) dt.
Evaluate displacement: x = v_0 t +  rac{1}{2} at^2.
For velocity-displacement relation, use a = v  rac{dv}{dx} Rightarrow a dx = v dv.
Integrate both sides: int_{0}^{x} a dx = int_{v_0}^{v} v dv Rightarrow ax =  rac{v^2 - v_0^2}{2} Rightarrow v^2 = v_0^2 + 2ax.

derivations.title: Derivation of Projectile Motion Trajectory Equation
derivations.conditions: Uniform gravitational acceleration acting downward, air resistance neglected.
steps: Resolve initial velocity v_0 into horizontal component u_x = v_0 cos	heta and vertical component u_y = v_0 sin	heta.
Write horizontal motion equation with zero acceleration: x = (v_0 cos	heta) t Rightarrow t =  rac{x}{v_0 cos	heta}.
Write vertical motion equation: y = (v_0 sin	heta) t -  rac{1}{2} g t^2.
Substitute the expression for time t into the vertical displacement equation:
y = (v_0 sin	heta) left( rac{x}{v_0 cos	heta}ight) -  rac{1}{2} g left( rac{x}{v_0 cos	heta}ight)^2.
Simplify the expression to obtain the equation of the trajectory in form y = ax - bx^2.
derivations.result: y = x 	an	heta -  rac{g x^2}{2 v_0^2 cos^2	heta}

graphs_and_experiments.title: Velocity-Time (v-t) Graph under Uniform Acceleration
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line sloping upwards with a positive slope from an intercept v_0 on the velocity axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the line represents acceleration (a =  rac{dv}{dt}), and the area under the v-t curve between two time instants represents total displacement.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via numerical interpretation of graph areas and finding instantaneous acceleration from slopes.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Acceleration-Time (a-t) Graph for Constant Acceleration
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A horizontal straight line parallel to the time axis at value a = c.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The area enclosed between the a-t curve and the time axis gives the change in velocity (Delta v) over that interval.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to test integration concepts for variable versus constant acceleration regimes.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Free-Fall Experiment (Drop Method)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Experimental setup diagram showing an electromagnet releasing a steel ball, photogate timers, and a free-fall column.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Verifies s =  rac{1}{2} gt^2 by plotting s versus t^2, yielding a straight line whose slope provides experimental g.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions on sources of error like air drag and reaction time.

solved_numericals.question: A train moving with a constant acceleration covers a distance of 64 m in 4 seconds and 120 m in 6 seconds. Find its initial velocity and acceleration.
solution_steps: Use second equation of motion: s = v_0 t +  rac{1}{2} at^2.
For first condition (s = 64, t = 4): 64 = 4v_0 +  rac{1}{2} a (16) Rightarrow 64 = 4v_0 + 8a Rightarrow 16 = v_0 + 2a (Equation 1).
For second condition (s = 120, t = 6): 120 = 6v_0 +  rac{1}{2} a (36) Rightarrow 120 = 6v_0 + 18a Rightarrow 20 = v_0 + 3a (Equation 2).
Subtract Equation 1 from Equation 2: (20 - 16) = (v_0 + 3a) - (v_0 + 2a) Rightarrow a = 4 m/s^2.
Substitute a into Equation 1: 16 = v_0 + 2(4) Rightarrow v_0 = 16 - 8 = 8 m/s.

solved_numericals.question: The acceleration of a particle moving along a straight line is given by a = 2t + 3, where a is in m/s^2 and t in seconds. If the particle starts from rest at x = 0 when t = 0, find its position at t = 3 seconds.
solution_steps: Write acceleration as a derivative of velocity:  rac{dv}{dt} = 2t + 3.
Integrate to find velocity function: v(t) = int (2t + 3) dt = t^2 + 3t + C_1.
Given particle starts from rest at t = 0 (v = 0), so C_1 = 0. Thus, v(t) = t^2 + 3t.
Write velocity as a derivative of position:  rac{dx}{dt} = t^2 + 3t.
Integrate to find position function: x(t) = int (t^2 + 3t) dt =  rac{t^3}{3} +  rac{3t^2}{2} + C_2.
Given x = 0 at t = 0, so C_2 = 0.

solved_numericals.question: A stone is dropped from the top of a tower of height h. At the same moment, another stone is projected vertically upward from the ground with speed u. If they meet halfway up the tower, find the time at which they meet and the height h in terms of u and g.
solution_steps: Let them meet at height h/2 from the ground at time t.
For the stone dropped from the top: initial velocity u_1 = 0, downward displacement y_1 = h -  rac{h}{2} =  rac{h}{2}. Using s = vt +  rac{1}{2}at^2:  rac{h}{2} =  rac{1}{2} gt^2 Rightarrow h = gt^2.
For the stone projected upward from the ground: upward displacement y_2 =  rac{h}{2}, initial velocity = u. Using s = ut -  rac{1}{2}gt^2:  rac{h}{2} = ut -  rac{1}{2}gt^2.
Substitute h = gt^2 into the second equation:  rac{gt^2}{2} = ut -  rac{1}{2}gt^2 Rightarrow gt^2 = ut.

Since t 
eq 0, time of meeting is t =  rac{u}{g}.
Substitute t back into h = gt^2: h = g left( rac{u}{g}ight)^2 =  rac{u^2}{g}.
solved_numericals.answer: Time t = u/g, Height h = u^2/g

assumptions_and_limitations: Standard kinematic equations assume constant acceleration unless explicitly integrated using variable calculus.
Macroscopic objects are treated as point masses, ignoring rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom unless specified.
Earth is assumed to be an inertial reference frame for elementary problems, though high-accuracy PGT problems may require accounting for non-inertial effects such as centrifugal and Coriolis forces.

common_misconceptions.wrong: An object thrown vertically upward has zero velocity and zero acceleration at its maximum height.
common_misconceptions.correct: Velocity is zero momentarily, but acceleration remains constant at g downward.
common_misconceptions.why: Gravity acts continuously regardless of the instantaneous magnitude or direction of velocity.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The equations of motion can be applied directly when acceleration varies with time.
common_misconceptions.correct: Standard SUVAT equations fail under variable acceleration; calculus integration must be used.
common_misconceptions.why: The derivation of standard kinematic formulas strictly requires the condition of constant acceleration.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Distance traveled in the n-th second is equal to the average velocity multiplied by n.
common_misconceptions.correct: Distance in the exact n-th second is given by S_n = v_0 +  rac{a}{2}(2n - 1).
common_misconceptions.why: Total distance in n seconds is different from the incremental displacement accrued during a single discrete one-second interval.

quick_revision: Always verify whether acceleration is constant before applying standard kinematic equations (v = u + at, s = ut + 1/2at^2, v^2 = u^2 + 2as).
For free fall, take downward as negative or positive consistently, ensuring sign convention for initial velocity, displacement, and g match.
In variable acceleration problems, always utilize definite integrals with proper initial boundary conditions for velocity and position.
